items.title: The earliest Christians thought Jesus would return within their lifetime
items.claim: Paul's letters (50s CE) are the oldest Christian texts. What does he tell his churches about the timing of Christ's return?

options.text: He explicitly warns that it will be many centuries away
He tells believers — in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 — that 'we who are alive, who are left' will be caught up to meet the Lord
He refuses to discuss the timing at all
He places the return precisely at AD 70, the destruction of the Temple

items.reveal:
1 Thessalonians 4:15-17, written around 50-51 CE, includes Paul among those still alive at the Parousia. 1 Corinthians 7:29 says 'the appointed time has grown short.' Mark 9:1 has Jesus saying 'some standing here will not taste death' before seeing the Kingdom.

When Christ did not return, later texts (e.g. 2 Peter 3:8 — 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years') reinterpret the delay. This shift is one of the central transformations of early Christian theology.
items.why: Treating the New Testament as a unified, settled doctrine misses that it documents a community reinterpreting itself in real time. The 'delay of the Parousia' is one of the formative pressures on Christian thought.

items.title: The Christian Bible's contents were not fixed until centuries after Christ
items.claim: When was the New Testament canon — the 27 books — first listed in its current form?

options.text: By the apostles themselves, before 70 CE
At the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE
Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 CE is the first surviving list of exactly the 27 books; consensus formed gradually through the 4th-5th centuries
By Pope Damasus I at the Council of Trent in 1546

items.reveal:
Athanasius of Alexandria's 39th Festal Letter (367 CE) is the first surviving document listing the 27 NT books we have today. Regional councils (Hippo 393, Carthage 397) confirmed it. The Trent council (1546) made it formal Catholic dogma — partly in response to the Reformation.

Nicaea (325) dealt with the Arian controversy, not the canon — a common confusion popularised by Dan Brown's 'The Da Vinci Code'.

Gospels left out include Thomas, Mary, Peter and the Infancy Gospel of James. Some books that nearly made it (the Shepherd of Hermas, 1 Clement) didn't.
items.why: The 'received text' image of Scripture obscures a long, contested human process. Knowing the canon was assembled doesn't disprove faith — but it changes the questions you can ask.

items.title: The Hebrew Bible barely mentions an afterlife
items.claim: What does the Hebrew Bible (the Christian Old Testament) say about heaven and hell?

options.text: It describes both in detail throughout
It mostly speaks of Sheol — a shadowy underworld where the dead exist as shades — with explicit resurrection only in late texts like Daniel 12
It denies any afterlife outright
It describes reincarnation in Genesis

items.reveal:
Job 3:13-19, Ecclesiastes 9:5-10 ('the dead know nothing') and the Psalms describe Sheol as a silent underworld common to all the dead. Daniel 12:2 (mid-2nd century BCE) is the clearest explicit resurrection passage — and it's one of the latest books.

By Jesus's time, Pharisees believed in resurrection and Sadducees did not (Mark 12:18-27). Christian heaven and hell as detailed afterlife destinations are largely shaped by intertestamental Jewish apocalyptic literature, Greek thought and later Christian elaboration (Dante most famously).
items.why: Students often assume the afterlife is a 'religious universal'. Within the Abrahamic tradition itself it's a developing idea, with the most familiar version being relatively recent.

items.title: Aristotle reached medieval Europe via Arabic translations
items.claim: Most of Aristotle's works were lost to Latin Europe by 500 CE. How did Aquinas (d. 1274) have access to them?

options.text: They had been continuously preserved in Vatican archives
Via Arabic translations and commentaries by Muslim scholars like Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Averroes (Ibn Rushd), re-translated into Latin in the 12th-13th centuries
Marco Polo brought them back from China
They were rediscovered in Constantinople after 1453

items.reveal:
From the 8th-10th centuries, the Abbasid Caliphate's 'House of Wisdom' (Bayt al-Hikma) in Baghdad sponsored translation of Greek philosophy and science into Arabic. Ibn Sina (Avicenna, d. 1037) and Ibn Rushd (Averroes, d. 1198) wrote major commentaries.

In 12th-century Toledo and Sicily, Christian, Jewish and Muslim scholars translated these Arabic texts into Latin. Aquinas's engagement with Aristotle relies heavily on Averroes (the 'Commentator'). Without that chain, scholastic philosophy as we know it would not exist.
items.why: Histories of European thought often skip the Islamic intermediary entirely. The intellectual map of medieval Europe makes no sense without it.

items.title: Buddhism has no creator god
items.claim: Does Buddhism teach the existence of a supreme creator deity?

options.text: Yes, the Buddha is the supreme deity worshipped as such
No — classical Buddhism rejects an eternal creator god; gods (devas) may exist but are themselves caught in samsara
Yes, Brahma is the Buddhist supreme being
Only Mahayana Buddhism affirms a creator god

items.reveal:
In the Pali Canon, the Buddha refuses metaphysical speculation about a creator (e.g. the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta, the 'parable of the poisoned arrow'). Devas exist but are impermanent and themselves seek liberation. The path to nibbana does not depend on grace from a supreme being.

Later traditions (Pure Land, some Mahayana schools) develop devotional practice toward Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but these are still not creators in the Abrahamic sense.

The Buddha is not a god — he is an awakened human teacher.
items.why: Western religious frameworks define 'religion' through theism. Buddhism is a major world tradition that fits awkwardly inside that frame — and forces a rethink of what 'religion' even means.

items.title: Nicaea was a political project as much as a theological one
items.claim: Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE. What was his primary motive?

options.text: Pure theological inquiry into the nature of Christ
Political unity — the empire had recently legalised Christianity, and the Arian controversy was fracturing the church
To remove gospels he personally disliked from the Bible
To suppress the worship of Mary

items.reveal:
Constantine had legalised Christianity by the Edict of Milan (313). The Arian controversy (was the Son co-eternal with the Father, or created?) threatened civil order. Constantine wrote to Bishop Alexander and Arius effectively telling them to stop arguing.

The Council produced the Nicene Creed and condemned Arius. Constantine was baptised on his deathbed in 337 — by an Arian bishop. Theological disputes continued for decades; Athanasius was exiled five times.

The Council did NOT decide the canon of Scripture (a persistent Dan Brown myth).
items.why: Doctrines aren't formed in a vacuum. Constantine wanted a workable state religion. The metaphysics of the Trinity took shape under that pressure — neither invalidating it nor making it 'pure theology'.

items.title: The Five Pillars of Islam have a strict canonical order
items.claim: What is the standard order of the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam?

options.text: Charity, fasting, prayer, pilgrimage, declaration
Shahada (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (almsgiving), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca, once if able)
Hajj, Salah, Sawm, Shahada, Zakat
There is no fixed order; lists vary by region

items.reveal:
The Hadith of Gabriel (recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) lists them in this order. The Shahada is the doorway — 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God'.

Shia Islam (Twelver tradition) frames the obligations differently — they recognise the practices but list them as part of the Ten Ancillaries (Furu al-Din), alongside jihad, enjoining good and forbidding wrong.

Zakat is typically 2.5% of accumulated wealth annually; Sawm requires no food, drink or marital relations from dawn to sunset in Ramadan.
items.why: Religious practice is not a generic 'doing good'. Islam has specific, ordered obligations with detailed theological rationale — exam answers that treat the Pillars as interchangeable miss the structure.

items.title: The Sunni-Shia split began as a political dispute about succession
items.claim: What is the origin of the Sunni-Shia division?

options.text: Two communities formed in different countries centuries apart

After Muhammad's death in 632 CE, the question of succession divided those who supported Abu Bakr (Sunni) from those who held Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, had been designated (Shia) — fully entrenched after the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala in 680 CE
A 19th-century theological dispute about scripture
A modern political invention with no early roots

items.reveal:
Muhammad died on 8 June 632 without naming a successor unambiguously. Abu Bakr was chosen as the first caliph; Ali became fourth caliph (656-661) after the assassinations of Umar and Uthman.

The First Fitna (civil war) and Husayn ibn Ali's death at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) crystallised Shia identity. The annual commemoration of Ashura mourns Husayn.

Today: around 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni, 10-15% Shia. Shia majorities: Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain. Significant minorities: Lebanon, Yemen, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India.
items.why: Religious traditions can be deeply shaped by political beginnings. The Sunni-Shia distinction is real and consequential — and originally a question about who should lead, not what to believe.

items.title: Muslims believe the Quran is the direct, unchanged word of God
items.claim: How do Muslims understand the origin of the Quran?

options.text: A collection of Muhammad's wise sayings, gathered over centuries
Revealed directly by God to Muhammad through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) over 23 years (610-632 CE), to be recited and transmitted unchanged in Arabic
A revised version of the Bible adapted for Arabia
A book written by Muhammad based on his teachings

items.reveal:
The word 'Quran' comes from the Arabic root q-r-' meaning 'to recite'. The first revelation (Sura 96, 'Iqra' — Recite!) at Mount Hira around 610 CE.

The Quran was compiled in written form under Caliph Uthman (around 650 CE), with non-conforming versions destroyed to ensure a single authoritative text. Muslims regard the Arabic text — not translations — as the Quran proper.

The Hadith (sayings of Muhammad) is a distinct category, recorded by his companions, with major Sunni collections by Bukhari (d. 870) and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 875).
items.why: The Quran's status differs sharply from how Christians treat the Bible (composed by human authors under divine inspiration). Islamic theology treats every Arabic word as direct divine speech — which is why translation is always a 'meaning of' the Quran.

items.title: Jihad means 'struggle' — and has a greater inner meaning
items.claim: What is the classical Islamic distinction between greater and lesser jihad?

options.text: Greater jihad is large-scale war; lesser jihad is small skirmishes

A widely cited hadith distinguishes the 'lesser jihad' (armed struggle in defence of the community) from the 'greater jihad' (the inner struggle against one's own ego) — though the hadith's authenticity is debated by some scholars
Jihad means only armed warfare; it has no inner meaning
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Scholars including Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and modern critics question the hadith's authenticity. But the inner-struggle understanding is found independently in Sufi traditions and in mainstream piety.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: Ramadan moves through the year because Islam uses a lunar calendar
items.claim: Why does Ramadan fall in different seasons across years?

options.text: It is set by Islamic council each year arbitrarily

The Islamic calendar is purely lunar, with no intercalation, so its 12 months total around 354 days — Ramadan shifts about 11 days earlier each Gregorian year, cycling through all seasons over around 33 years
It follows the solar year like Western religions
It is fixed to August every year

items.reveal:
Most other religious calendars (Jewish, Hindu, Buddhist) are lunisolar — they add intercalary months to stay tied to the solar year. The Islamic (Hijri) calendar deliberately rejects intercalation, based on Quran 9:36-37.

The Hijri year begins from Muhammad's emigration (hijra) from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. The Hijri year 1446 began in July 2024.

Ramadan in tropical countries near the equator stays around 12-14 hours of fasting; in summer in high latitudes it can reach 20+ hours, raising practical questions for which scholars give differing rulings.
items.why: Calendar choices have theological consequences. The Islamic refusal to align the lunar year with the seasons produces a religious experience that cycles through climates and conditions — different in design from Christianity or Judaism.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible
items.claim: What is the Torah?

options.text: The entire Old Testament
The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash
Only the book of Genesis
A modern compilation of prayers

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) has three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). Tanakh is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in a one-year cycle (annual cycle) or three-year cycle (some Reform congregations). The annual cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' as a generic term for Jewish scripture obscures structure. Students need to distinguish Torah, Tanakh and Talmud — and notice that Christian 'Old Testament' is the same content as Tanakh but in different order.

items.title: Judaism centres on covenant — a binding agreement with God
items.claim: What is the relationship between the Abrahamic and Mosaic covenants in Judaism?

options.text: One covenant replaced the other
The Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17, sealed by circumcision) promises land and descendants; the Mosaic covenant (Exodus 19-24, at Sinai) gives the Torah law — both remain binding on Jews
There is only one covenant — at Sinai
Covenants applied only to ancient Israelites, not modern Jews

items.reveal:
Brit milah (covenant of circumcision) is performed on Jewish boys on the eighth day after birth, marking the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:11-13). The Mosaic covenant at Sinai (around 1300 BCE in traditional dating) establishes the 613 mitzvot (commandments) of the Torah law.

The Noahide covenant (Genesis 9) — applying to all humanity — is also recognised. Rabbinic Judaism distinguishes seven Noahide laws binding on all people from the 613 mitzvot binding specifically on Jews.

Christianity reinterprets these covenants through 'new covenant' theology (Hebrews 8); Judaism rejects supersessionism — the older covenants are not abrogated.
items.why: Covenant is not a vague concept of relationship. In Judaism it is a specific structure with terms, obligations and consequences — and a major point of theological disagreement with Christianity.

items.title: Kosher rules separate meat and dairy
items.claim: What are the main categories of kosher (kashrut) restrictions?

options.text: Only vegetarian foods are permitted

Permitted animals (mammals that chew cud and have cloven hooves; fish with fins and scales); ritual slaughter (shechita); separation of meat and dairy in cooking, eating and utensils; specific prohibitions including pork, shellfish, mixing milk and meat
Only meals at synagogue must be kosher
Kosher refers only to wine

items.reveal:
The meat-dairy separation derives from three repetitions of 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). Rabbinic interpretation extended this to all mixing of meat and dairy.

Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 list permitted and forbidden animals. Pork and shellfish are the most widely known prohibitions; rabbit, camel and birds of prey are also forbidden.

Shechita is ritual slaughter by a trained shochet with a perfectly sharp knife in a single cut — designed to be quick and to drain blood. Some European countries (Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Belgian regions) have banned shechita without prior stunning on animal welfare grounds.
items.why: Religious practice is often embodied — daily eating, household kitchens, separate dishes. Kashrut is one of the clearest cases of belief expressed through bodily and domestic practice.

items.title: Modern Judaism has three or four main branches
items.claim: What are the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: One unified Judaism with no internal divisions

Orthodox (including Modern Orthodox and Haredi); Conservative (called Masorti in UK); Reform; Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and the role of modernity
Catholic and Protestant Jews
Only ethnic, not religious, divisions exist

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Orthodox responses (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging with modern life.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel, the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in different ways.

items.title: Shabbat begins on Friday evening, not Saturday
items.claim: When does the Jewish Sabbath begin and end?

options.text: It runs from Saturday morning to Sunday morning
From sunset on Friday to the appearance of three stars on Saturday night — Jewish days begin at sunset, following Genesis 1's 'and there was evening and there was morning'
It is calculated by the Gregorian clock
It runs all weekend continuously

items.reveal:
The Genesis creation account marks each day 'there was evening and there was morning' — establishing the Jewish day as evening to evening. Shabbat is welcomed with candle lighting (typically 18 minutes before sunset) and Kiddush over wine.

The Torah commands rest from melacha — 39 categories of work derived from the activities involved in building the Tabernacle. These include lighting fires, writing, carrying in public, tearing, cooking. Modern applications (electricity, driving, mobile phones) follow rabbinic reasoning by analogy.

Shabbat ends with Havdalah — a brief ceremony with wine, spices and a multi-wick candle separating the holy from the ordinary.
items.why: Religious time is structured differently. Treating Shabbat as 'Saturday' misses both its beginning at sunset and the depth of its observance — which is one of the most distinctive elements of Jewish practice.

items.title: The Four Noble Truths are the Buddha's core teaching
items.claim: What are the Four Noble Truths?

options.text: Compassion, generosity, mindfulness, patience
Dukkha (suffering exists), Samudaya (its cause is craving/tanha), Nirodha (it can cease), Magga (the path — the Eightfold Path)
Birth, illness, ageing, death
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort

items.reveal:
The Buddha is said to have taught the Four Noble Truths in his first sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) at Sarnath, near Varanasi, after his enlightenment. They are framed as a medical diagnosis: symptom, cause, prognosis, treatment.

'Dukkha' is often translated 'suffering' but more accurately covers unsatisfactoriness, impermanence, the inability of conditioned things to give lasting peace. 'Tanha' is craving — including for existence and non-existence, not just for pleasure.

The Eightfold Path (the Fourth Noble Truth) is grouped into wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, action, livelihood) and mental discipline (right effort, mindfulness, concentration).
items.why: Buddhism is often summarised as 'life is suffering' — a misleading reduction. The Four Noble Truths are a structured argument from problem to solution, not a pessimistic mood.

items.title: Nirvana is not heaven — it is the cessation of craving
items.claim: How does Buddhism understand nirvana (nibbana in Pali)?

options.text: A paradisiacal afterlife realm
The 'blowing out' of the fires of greed, hatred and delusion — the end of suffering and rebirth, attainable in this life as well as at death (parinirvana)
Reunion with a supreme deity
A meditative trance state achieved daily

items.reveal:
The Pali 'nibbana' / Sanskrit 'nirvana' literally means 'blowing out' — as a flame is extinguished. The image is from the Adittapariyaya Sutta (Fire Sermon).

Nirvana attained in life is sometimes distinguished from parinirvana — the full nirvana at death of an enlightened being. The Buddha attained nirvana under the Bodhi tree (around age 35) and parinirvana around age 80.

The Buddha refused to speculate about nirvana's metaphysical status — whether the enlightened being exists, doesn't exist, both or neither after death (Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta). Speculation does not lead to liberation.
items.why: Translating nirvana as 'heaven' imports Christian assumptions. The Buddhist concept is structurally different — not a destination but an end, not a reward but a release.

items.title: Buddhism rejects the existence of a permanent self
items.claim: What is the Buddhist teaching of anatta?

options.text: The soul is eternal and unchanging
There is no permanent, unchanging self (atman); what we call 'self' is a constantly changing aggregation of five skandhas (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness)
Only the body is real; the soul is illusion
Each person has multiple souls

items.reveal:
Anatta (no-self) is one of the three marks of existence in Buddhism, alongside anicca (impermanence) and dukkha (unsatisfactoriness). The doctrine sharply distinguishes Buddhism from Hinduism's atman/Brahman teaching.

The Anattalakkhana Sutta — the Buddha's second sermon — argues each of the five skandhas is impermanent and not under our control, so cannot be 'self'.

Later Mahayana schools developed the concept further. Yogacara introduced 'alaya-vijnana' (storehouse consciousness); some Pure Land traditions speak of 'Buddha-nature' that complicates the picture without abandoning anatta.
items.why: Anatta is one of the most counter-intuitive religious doctrines. It contradicts both Western theological assumptions about the soul and lived experience of continuity — and is the central philosophical claim of Buddhism.

items.title: Theravada and Mahayana are two major Buddhist traditions
items.claim: What distinguishes the major Buddhist schools?

options.text: There are no real differences between Buddhist schools

Theravada ('teaching of the elders', dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos) emphasises individual liberation through the Pali Canon; Mahayana (East Asia, Vietnam) emphasises the bodhisattva path and includes Pure Land, Zen and Tibetan (Vajrayana) traditions
Theravada is Buddhist; Mahayana is a separate religion
Both are identical to Hinduism

items.reveal:
The split developed in the centuries after the Buddha's death, with the Second Council (around 100 years after his parinirvana) marking early disagreements. Mahayana texts (Prajnaparamita Sutras, Lotus Sutra) emerged from around the 1st century BCE.

The bodhisattva ideal — postponing one's own final liberation to help all beings — is central to Mahayana. Theravada acknowledges bodhisattvas (including the historical Buddha before his enlightenment) but emphasises the arhat ideal (the awakened practitioner).

Tibetan Buddhism is sometimes treated as a separate Vajrayana branch. Zen and Pure Land are East Asian Mahayana developments.
items.why: Calling Buddhism 'one religion' obscures real diversity. Theravada and Mahayana share core teachings but differ on the path, the goal, the texts treated as authoritative, and the role of devotion.

items.title: Hindu philosophy teaches the unity of atman and Brahman
items.claim: What is the relationship between atman and Brahman in Vedantic Hinduism?

options.text: They are completely separate — the soul and a creator god

The Upanishads teach that atman (the individual self) and Brahman (ultimate reality) are one — 'tat tvam asi' ('that thou art', Chandogya Upanishad). Different Vedanta schools interpret the relationship variously (non-dual, qualified non-dual, dualist)
Atman is illusion; only Brahman is real, with no relation between them
Brahman is a god subordinate to atman

items.reveal:
The Mahavakyas ('great sayings') include 'tat tvam asi' (Chandogya 6.8.7), 'aham brahmasmi' (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10) and 'ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2).

Shankara (8th century CE) developed Advaita Vedanta — non-duality: atman is identical to Brahman; perceived multiplicity is maya (illusion).

Ramanuja (11th-12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita — qualified non-duality: atman is a real attribute of Brahman but distinct. Madhva (13th century) taught Dvaita — full dualism: souls and God are eternally distinct.

All three schools are valid orthodox Vedantic positions.
items.why: Hindu philosophy of self is sophisticated. Treating Hinduism as 'just polytheism' misses the metaphysical core that has shaped Indian thought for over two millennia.

items.title: Samsara, karma and moksha are linked in Hindu cosmology
items.claim: How do samsara, karma and moksha relate?

options.text: They are unrelated concepts
Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; karma is the moral causation that drives it; moksha is liberation from the cycle — typically by realising the unity of atman and Brahman
Karma punishes the wicked in this life only
Moksha is automatic at death for all souls

items.reveal:
Karma (action) produces fruits (phala) that bind the soul to future rebirths. Bad karma leads to lower rebirths (animal, hell realms); good karma to better ones (human, deva). All rebirth is conditioned and impermanent.

Moksha is the exit from samsara — variously achieved through jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (right action), or yoga (meditation). The Bhagavad Gita presents all four as legitimate paths.

Buddhism shares samsara, karma and liberation concepts but rejects atman — so 'rebirth' in Buddhism is the continuation of a causal stream, not a soul transmigrating.
items.why: Indian-origin religions share a family of concepts that differ in detail but contrast structurally with Abrahamic religions. The cyclic worldview shapes everything from ethics to attitudes towards death.

items.title: Hindu deities are often manifestations of one ultimate reality
items.claim: How does Hindu theology relate the many gods to Brahman?

options.text: Each god is wholly separate and independent

Many Hindus understand the gods as manifestations (devas) of one ultimate reality (Brahman) — though the relationship varies between traditions, and some bhakti movements emphasise a personal supreme deity (Vishnu, Shiva, Devi)
There is only one god in Hinduism — Brahma
Hinduism is strictly atheist

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda (1.164.46) says 'Truth is one; sages call it by many names.' The Trimurti (Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer) is one classical way of mapping cosmic functions.

Vaishnavism centres on Vishnu and his avatars (Rama, Krishna). Shaivism centres on Shiva. Shaktism centres on Devi/Shakti (the divine feminine, including Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati). Each tradition may treat its chosen deity as supreme.

The term 'henotheism' (worshipping one god while acknowledging others) was coined by Max Müller in the 19th century specifically to describe Vedic religion.
items.why: Calling Hinduism polytheistic or monotheistic both miss the structure. The 'many manifestations of one' framework is philosophically distinct — and shapes how Hindus actually relate to images and shrines.

items.title: Caste is a complex social hierarchy with religious framings
items.claim: How does the caste system relate to Hindu religion?

options.text: It is purely social with no religious dimension

Varna (the fourfold theoretical division — Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras) is described in the Vedas and the Manusmriti; jati (thousands of birth-based occupational groupings) is the lived reality; modern reform movements (Ambedkar, Gandhi, contemporary Dalit activism) have contested its religious basis
Caste was invented by British colonisers
Caste applies only to non-Hindus

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta (10.90) describes the four varnas emerging from a cosmic being. The Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE-200 CE) codifies caste duties.

Dalits (formerly 'untouchables') were treated as outside the varna system. B.R. Ambedkar (1891-1956), Dalit leader and chief architect of India's constitution, converted to Buddhism in 1956 partly to escape caste. The Indian Constitution (1950) outlaws untouchability.

The relationship between varna theory and the thousands of jatis on the ground is complex. Caste discrimination persists in many forms — the UK Equality Act 2010 includes caste under race discrimination provisions.
items.why: Religious texts and social systems interact in ways that resist clean separation. The caste case shows how a religious tradition can be deployed for social hierarchy and also generate its own critics.

items.title: Sikhism was founded in 1469 by Guru Nanak
items.claim: What was Guru Nanak's central teaching?

options.text: A synthesis of Hinduism and Buddhism

One God (Ek Onkar), equality of all people, honest work (kirat karna), sharing with others (vand chakna), remembrance of God (naam japna) — rejecting caste, ritualism and religious exclusivism of his time
A reformed branch of Islam
A purely philosophical movement with no religious claims

items.reveal_title: There is neither Hindu nor Muslim
items.reveal:
Born in 1469 at Nankana Sahib (now in Pakistan), Nanak had a transformative spiritual experience in 1499. After emerging from three days at the Bein river he reportedly said 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — pointing past religious labels to a shared underlying truth.

He undertook four major journeys (udasis) across India, into Tibet, the Middle East and possibly to Mecca. He died in 1539.

The Mool Mantar — Sikhism's foundational statement — begins 'Ik Onkar': there is one God. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with this affirmation.
items.why: Sikhism is the youngest of the major Indian religions — a deliberate rethinking of religious identity in Mughal-era Punjab. Its founding moment is well-attested historically, unlike older religions.

items.title: There were ten human Sikh Gurus — the eleventh is the scripture
items.claim: How does the Sikh tradition handle leadership after Guru Gobind Singh?

options.text: It ended after the tenth Guru with no continuation
In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh declared the Guru Granth Sahib (the scripture) to be the eternal Guru — no further human gurus
It continues through a hereditary line
Multiple gurus operate simultaneously

items.reveal:
Guru Gobind Singh died in 1708 from a stab wound inflicted by an Afghan assassin. Before his death he installed the Adi Granth (compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604) as Guru Granth Sahib — making the scripture the eternal Guru.

The Guru Granth Sahib (1,430 pages, mostly in Gurmukhi script) contains hymns by six of the ten Gurus, plus 15 other Hindu and Muslim saints (bhagats) — including Kabir and Sheikh Farid. It is treated as a living Guru: bowed to, awakened in the morning, put to rest at night.

Sikh gurdwaras have the Guru Granth Sahib on a throne (palki) as the central focus.
items.why: The structural innovation of designating scripture as eternal Guru ended succession disputes that plague many religions. Sikh community continuity rests on the text, not on a living hierarchy.

items.title: The Khalsa was founded at Vaisakhi 1699
items.claim: What did Guru Gobind Singh establish in 1699?

options.text: A new Sikh state in northern India
The Khalsa (the 'pure') — a community of initiated Sikhs marked by the Five Ks (Kesh, Kara, Kanga, Kachera, Kirpan), open to all castes and gender
A revised version of the Guru Granth Sahib
A peace treaty with the Mughal Empire

items.reveal:
At Anandpur on Vaisakhi (April) 1699, Guru Gobind Singh called for volunteers willing to die for the faith. The Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) came forward, were initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword), and were then themselves used to initiate Gobind Singh.

The Five Ks: Kesh (uncut hair, including the dastaar turban), Kara (steel bracelet), Kanga (wooden comb), Kachera (cotton undergarment), Kirpan (small sword).

The Khalsa took the surname Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women — symbolically equalising caste and gender.
items.why: Sikh identity has visible bodily markers that emerged from a specific 1699 event with named participants. The Five Ks are not vague cultural symbols but coded responses to Mughal-era persecution and caste hierarchy.

items.title: Every Sikh gurdwara serves a free meal to all visitors
items.claim: What is langar?

options.text: A meal sold to support the gurdwara

A free communal meal served to anyone regardless of religion, caste, gender or background — a foundational Sikh practice, originated by Guru Nanak, institutionalised by Guru Amar Das (3rd Guru) who required visitors to eat langar before meeting him
An annual festival meal only
A meal restricted to initiated Khalsa Sikhs

items.reveal:
Langar is served in the langar hall of every gurdwara worldwide. All sit on the floor at the same level to eat — explicitly rejecting caste hierarchy. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar) serves around 100,000 meals daily; volunteers prepare and clean.

Guru Amar Das (1479-1574) made eating langar a requirement before meeting him — including for the Mughal Emperor Akbar, who reportedly sat with peasants before being granted an audience.

In the UK, Sikh organisations like Khalsa Aid extend the langar tradition to refugees, food banks and disaster response — recently in Ukraine, Turkey, and at UK floods.
items.why: Practice can teach doctrine. The simple physical act of sitting on the floor and eating together puts equality into the body — more direct than verbal teaching.

items.title: Aquinas offered five arguments for God, not one
items.claim: What are Aquinas's 'Five Ways'?

options.text: A single ontological argument
Five distinct arguments from observation: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer) — in Summa Theologiae I.2.3
Five biblical proofs only
Five mystical experiences

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes 'a priori' arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from 'a posteriori' arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move and change; an unmoved mover is required to start the chain. Second Way (efficient causation): everything has a cause; a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised individually. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's response to Copleston challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.

items.title: Anselm's ontological argument is a priori
items.claim: What is Anselm's ontological argument (Proslogion, 1078)?

options.text: An empirical argument from observation of nature
God is 'that than which no greater can be conceived'; existence in reality is greater than existence in the mind alone; therefore the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality
A historical argument from biblical events
An argument from religious experience

items.reveal:
Anselm wrote the Proslogion (1077-78) as a contemplation aimed at finding 'a single argument' to prove God's existence. The famous formula appears in Proslogion 2.

Gaunilo (Anselm's contemporary) objected with his 'lost island' parody: by the same logic, the greatest conceivable island must exist. Anselm replied that the argument applies only to a necessary being, not contingent ones.

Descartes (Meditations V), Spinoza, Leibniz and Hegel reformulated versions. Kant's critique — existence is not a predicate (Critique of Pure Reason, 1781) — is the standard counter. Alvin Plantinga's modal version (1974) revived the argument using possible-world semantics.
items.why: The ontological argument is uniquely controversial. Almost everyone has the intuition that something is wrong with it — but the precise diagnosis (Gaunilo's? Kant's? Modal logic?) is itself contested philosophy.

items.title: Paley's watchmaker argument was published in 1802
items.claim: What is Paley's analogy?

options.text: If we found a stone on a heath, we would infer no designer
If we found a watch on a heath, the complexity and purposive arrangement of its parts would compel us to infer a watchmaker — and similar reasoning applied to nature implies a divine designer
Nature is too random to need a designer
The argument compares the universe to a clockwork mechanism explicitly

items.reveal:
William Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) opens with the watch-on-the-heath analogy. He uses the human eye as his prime biological example.

Hume's 'Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion' (1779, published posthumously) anticipated and refuted versions of the design argument decades earlier — the analogy is weak (the universe is not like a watch), there are flaws (suggesting an apprentice designer or a committee), and the argument cannot reach a single benevolent God.

Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) provided a non-design explanation for biological complexity. Modern Intelligent Design (Behe, Dembski, 1990s onwards) is a controversial attempt to revive the argument scientifically.
items.why: The design argument keeps returning in new forms. Each version has to deal with the next development in science — biological evolution, cosmic fine-tuning, multiverse cosmology — making it a moving target rather than a settled debate.

items.title: Moral and natural evil are distinct problems
items.claim: What is the distinction between moral and natural evil?

options.text: All evil is caused by human moral failure

Moral evil is caused by free moral agents (murder, torture, cruelty); natural evil is caused by impersonal natural processes (earthquakes, disease, predation). They raise different problems for theism
All evil is illusion
Natural evil is just a subset of moral evil

items.reveal:
Free Will Defence (Augustine, Alvin Plantinga) explains moral evil as the cost of human free will — but doesn't obviously address natural evil. Earthquakes do not flow from human choices.

Irenaean theodicy (revived by John Hick, 'Evil and the God of Love', 1966) sees natural evil as part of soul-making — character development requires a challenging environment.

Augustinian theodicy treats evil as privatio boni (privation of good) — not a substance but an absence. The Fall extends moral consequences into nature.

The logical problem of evil (Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', 1955) has been largely answered by Plantinga; the evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979) remains live.
items.why: The problem of evil is the most persistent challenge to classical theism. Its sub-distinctions (moral/natural, logical/evidential) shape which theodicies are even relevant — and a generic answer misses the structure of the argument.

items.title: Wittgenstein's later work treated religious language as a 'language game'
items.claim: How did the later Wittgenstein approach religious language?

options.text: He argued religious language is meaningless

Religious language is a 'language game' embedded in a 'form of life' — it has its own grammar and logic, not reducible to scientific or empirical assertion. It is meaningful within its practice, regardless of whether it asserts external facts
He defended a literal cognitive interpretation
He treated all language games as equally true

items.reveal:
Wittgenstein's 'Philosophical Investigations' (published 1953) replaced the picture theory of meaning from his earlier 'Tractatus' (1921) with a use-theory. 'The meaning of a word is its use in the language.'

Religious language games — prayer, worship, doctrinal assertion — function differently from scientific language games. D.Z. Phillips and Norman Malcolm developed Wittgensteinian philosophy of religion in the 20th century.

Critics (Antony Flew, 'Theology and Falsification' 1950) argued this 'reduces' religious claims to non-cognitive expressions — but Wittgenstein himself was more nuanced, refusing both literalist and reductionist readings.
items.why: The 20th-century philosophy of religion shifted from 'do these claims correspond to reality?' to 'what kind of claims are these?'. Wittgenstein's move opens space for religious practice without requiring scientific-style verification.

items.title: Act and rule utilitarianism give different answers
items.claim: What is the distinction between act and rule utilitarianism?

options.text: They are alternative names for the same theory

Act utilitarianism judges each action by its consequences directly; rule utilitarianism asks which rules, if generally followed, would produce the greatest happiness — and applies those rules even when an individual act might seem to maximise utility differently
Rule utilitarianism rejects consequences entirely
Act utilitarianism is the only legitimate form

items.reveal:
Jeremy Bentham's 'Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789) introduced the hedonic calculus. John Stuart Mill's 'Utilitarianism' (1861) distinguished higher and lower pleasures.

Rule utilitarianism (developed by R.M. Hare and Richard Brandt in the 20th century) attempts to address objections to act utilitarianism — that it permits horrific acts (killing one innocent to save five) and creates impossible decision burdens.

Critics argue rule utilitarianism collapses into act utilitarianism (just add 'except in special cases') or into Kantian deontology (just follow the rules).
items.why: Utilitarianism is not one theory. The act/rule distinction changes the answers radically — and exam answers that treat 'utilitarianism' as monolithic miss the most important internal debate.

items.title: Kant gave multiple formulations of the categorical imperative
items.claim: How does Kant's categorical imperative work?

options.text: One simple rule: do unto others as you would have them do to you

Multiple formulations including universalisability ('act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law') and humanity-as-end ('act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only')
Whatever maximises happiness is morally required
An empirical rule derived from observation

items.reveal:
Kant's 'Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals' (1785) sets out the categorical imperative. Standard count: three formulations.

Formula of Universal Law: 'Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.'
Formula of Humanity: 'Act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only.'
Formula of the Kingdom of Ends: 'Act according to the maxims of a member of a merely possible kingdom of ends.'

The formulations are intended to be equivalent in extension but to emphasise different aspects. Kant's most famous example (lying to the murderer at the door) shows the strict reading: lying is universally impermissible.
items.why: Kantian ethics is sometimes reduced to 'don't lie' or 'universalise your action'. The multiple formulations and the humanity-as-end principle are richer — and more humane — than the slogan suggests.

items.title: Aristotelian virtue ethics aims at eudaimonia, not just being virtuous
items.claim: What is eudaimonia in Aristotle's ethics?

options.text: A momentary feeling of happiness

Flourishing or living well — the proper end of human life. The virtues (excellences of character) are dispositions that enable a person to function well as a human being and so to live a flourishing life
Wealth and reputation
Religious salvation

items.reveal:
Aristotle's 'Nicomachean Ethics' (Book I) argues that all human action aims at some good, and there must be a highest good — eudaimonia.

The ergon (function) argument: humans, like everything, have a characteristic function — rational activity according to virtue. The virtues are not lists of good behaviours but stable dispositions developed through habituation.

The doctrine of the mean: each virtue is between two vices (courage between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between miserliness and profligacy).

Alasdair MacIntyre's 'After Virtue' (1981) revived virtue ethics by arguing that modern moral discourse has lost the framework that gives moral vocabulary its meaning.
items.why: Virtue ethics is not 'be a good person'. It is a structured theory with specific terms — function, habituation, the mean, flourishing — that link character to the good life in a way that act-based theories don't.

items.title: Natural Law has primary and secondary precepts
items.claim: What are Aquinas's primary precepts of natural law?

options.text: Ten commandments derived from Exodus

Five primary precepts identified by Aquinas: preservation of life, reproduction, education of offspring, living in society, worship of God — secondary precepts (specific moral rules) are derived from them by reason
A single rule: do good and avoid evil
Only one precept — protect life

items.reveal:
Aquinas's natural law theory appears in the Summa Theologiae I-II (Questions 90-97). The eternal law is God's plan; natural law is rational creatures' participation in it; human law derives specific rules.

The doctrine of double effect — an action with a foreseen bad consequence can be permissible if the bad effect is not intended, the act itself is not intrinsically wrong, and the good outweighs the bad — is a key application (used in modern bioethics).

Natural law is the basis of Catholic moral teaching on contraception, abortion and end-of-life care. John Finnis and Germain Grisez developed 'New Natural Law' (from 1980) updating the framework.
items.why: Catholic ethics is not arbitrary doctrine — it rests on a developed rational framework. Engaging with natural law requires understanding the structure (primary, secondary, double effect) rather than treating it as a list of forbidden actions.

items.title: Joseph Fletcher's situation ethics centres on agape
items.claim: What is the central principle of Fletcher's situation ethics?

options.text: There are no moral rules of any kind
The single absolute is agape (selfless love); all other rules are guidelines that can be overridden when love requires it. Set out in 'Situation Ethics: The New Morality' (1966)
Maximise pleasure for the greatest number
Always follow biblical commands literally

items.reveal:
Fletcher's six propositions: (1) Only love is intrinsically good. (2) The ruling norm of Christian decision is love, not law. (3) Love and justice are the same — justice is love distributed. (4) Love wills the neighbour's good. (5) Only the end justifies the means. (6) Love's decisions are made situationally, not prescriptively.

Fletcher gave four working principles: pragmatism, relativism, positivism, personalism.

The Vatican condemned situation ethics under Pius XII (1956, before Fletcher's book) and again in the 1990s. Critics argue that 'love' as the only criterion is too vague to guide decisions; defenders argue agape has specific content (the New Testament's understanding) that excludes self-interested 'love'.
items.why: Christian ethics in the mid-20th century split between absolutist and contextual approaches. Fletcher's situation ethics is a high-profile example of context-driven ethics — challenging the natural law tradition from within Christianity.

items.title: Pesach commemorates the Exodus from Egypt
items.claim: What does Pesach (Passover) celebrate?

options.text: The giving of the Torah at Sinai
The Exodus from Egyptian slavery — the angel of death 'passing over' Jewish homes marked with lamb's blood, the hasty departure (unleavened bread), the crossing of the Red Sea
The destruction of the Second Temple
The autumn harvest

items.reveal:
Pesach falls on 15 Nisan (March-April). It lasts 7 days in Israel (Reform Jews observe 7 days worldwide), 8 days in the Diaspora (Orthodox/Conservative).

The Seder is the ritual meal on the first night (and second night outside Israel). The Haggadah ('the telling') is the text recited — recounting the Exodus story through symbolic foods (matzah, maror, charoset), four cups of wine, and the four questions.

'Next year in Jerusalem' closes the Seder. The festival's themes of liberation have shaped social movements: the African American spiritual tradition (Go Down Moses), the Civil Rights movement (King invoked Exodus), liberation theology.
items.why: Judaism's major festivals carry specific historical content. Pesach is not generic 'spring festival' but a structured ritual recreation of a specific liberation narrative — central to Jewish identity for over two millennia.

items.title: Ashura commemorates Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala
items.claim: What is the significance of Ashura in Shia Islam?

options.text: A celebration of victory in battle
Commemoration of the martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali (grandson of Muhammad) at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) — a defining event of Shia identity, marked with mourning rituals
The Prophet Muhammad's birthday
Only a Sunni festival

items.reveal:
Husayn, his family and 72 followers refused allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid I and were besieged then killed at Karbala (in modern Iraq). The event is recounted in detail in Shia narrative tradition (maqtal literature).

Muharram processions (matam) in Shia communities involve mourning, recitation, sometimes ritualised self-flagellation (different observances by region; many Shia clerics prefer blood donation as a modern alternative).

In Sunni Islam, 10 Muharram is also significant — Muhammad observed the day as a fast, having found Jewish residents of Medina fasting in commemoration of Moses's deliverance. Sunni observance is much quieter than Shia.
items.why: Religious calendars carry historical memory. Ashura, like Pesach, ritualises a specific historical wound — and the difference in how Sunnis and Shias mark the same date reveals the structural differences between the branches.

items.title: Diwali has multiple regional meanings
items.claim: What does Diwali celebrate?

options.text: A single event — Rama's return to Ayodhya

Multiple events depending on region: Rama's return to Ayodhya (north India), Krishna's defeat of Narakasura (south India), Lakshmi's emergence (west India); also marks new year for some Hindu, Jain and Sikh communities
Only the Hindu new year
A purely Sikh festival

items.reveal:
Diwali (Sanskrit dipavali, 'row of lamps') falls in October-November on the new moon of Kartika. The five-day festival includes Dhanteras (wealth), Naraka Chaturdashi (Krishna's victory), Diwali itself (Lakshmi puja, Rama's return), Govardhan Puja, and Bhai Dooj (siblings).

For Jains, it marks Mahavira's attainment of moksha. For Sikhs, it commemorates Guru Hargobind's release from imprisonment in 1619 (Bandi Chhor Divas).

The festival has become a major UK public event — Leicester's Diwali celebrations are the largest outside India.
items.why: Pan-Hindu festivals can have different narratives in different regions. Treating Diwali as a single myth misses how diverse Hindu practice is and how it links to neighbouring traditions (Jain, Sikh) at the same calendrical moment.

items.title: Buddhism has four 'divine abodes' to cultivate
items.claim: What are the four brahma viharas (divine abodes) in Buddhism?

options.text: Four meditative postures
Metta (loving-kindness), karuna (compassion), mudita (sympathetic joy), upekkha (equanimity) — qualities to be developed towards oneself and all beings
Four directions to face when meditating
Four Buddhist holidays

items.reveal:
The brahma viharas appear in the Metta Sutta and elsewhere in the Pali Canon. Each has a 'far enemy' (opposite) and a 'near enemy' (resembling counterfeit): metta vs. ill-will (far) and selfish affection (near); compassion vs. cruelty and pity.

Metta meditation begins with oneself, extends to loved ones, then to neutral persons, then to enemies, then to all beings. It is one of the most widely taught meditations in modern mindfulness and secular contexts.

The brahma viharas are practical training, not theological doctrine — they can be practised by Buddhists and non-Buddhists.
items.why: Buddhist ethics is not primarily about rules. It is about training specific mental qualities. Engaging with Buddhism academically requires understanding this training-oriented framework — quite different from command-based Abrahamic ethics.

items.title: British religious affiliation has dropped sharply since the 1960s
items.claim: What does the 2021 UK Census show about religion?

options.text: Christianity remains the majority belief

For the first time, less than half of England and Wales (46.2%) identified as Christian; 37.2% had no religion; Islam grew to 6.5%; Hindu, Sikh, Jewish, Buddhist and Other religions made up the remainder
Religion has grown overall
All religions are at the same percentage

items.reveal:
The 2001 Census recorded 72% Christian; 2011 recorded 59%; 2021 recorded 46% in England and Wales. The 'no religion' category rose from 15% (2001) to 25% (2011) to 37% (2021). Scotland (2022 census) showed similar trends; Northern Ireland remains more religious.

Muslim population: 3% (2001), 5% (2011), 6.5% (2021).

Secularisation theory (Bryan Wilson, Peter Berger) predicted declining religious influence with modernity. The reality has been more complex — declining institutional affiliation alongside persistent or growing 'spiritual but not religious' identification and increasing pluralism.
items.why: British religion is restructured, not just declining. The Census numbers show a more religiously plural country where institutional Christianity has lost its majority position — major implications for education, ethics and public life.

items.title: William James identified four marks of mystical experience
items.claim: What are James's four marks of mystical experience?

options.text: Sight, sound, touch, taste

Ineffability (cannot be fully described), noetic quality (provides knowledge), transiency (does not last long), passivity (the subject feels acted upon) — set out in 'The Varieties of Religious Experience' (1902)
Joy, peace, love, hope
Prayer, meditation, study, fasting

items.reveal:
James's Gifford Lectures (1901-02) became 'The Varieties of Religious Experience'. He aimed to study religion empirically as a phenomenon of consciousness, regardless of any metaphysical truth claims.

His four marks were intended as descriptive criteria, not arguments for divine reality. Richard Swinburne ('The Existence of God', 1979) and others later used religious experience evidentially — the principle of credulity (we should believe perceptions unless we have reason not to) and the principle of testimony.

Critics including Walter Kaufmann and Steven Katz have argued that mystical experience is heavily shaped by prior cultural framework — a Buddhist's experience is structured by Buddhist concepts.
items.why: Religious experience is studied both descriptively (what do people report?) and evaluatively (what does it prove?). James's framework remains the starting point for both — a century of subsequent debate has built on his typology.

items.title: Confucianism is not always classed as a religion
items.claim: How is Confucianism typically classified?

options.text: A monotheistic religion with a creator god

An ethical and philosophical tradition centred on social relationships and self-cultivation — often called a religion in Western frameworks but treated as philosophy and ethics in Chinese tradition; rituals (li) and the cultivation of virtues (ren, yi, zhi, xin) are central
A modern political movement only
Identical to Taoism

items.reveal:
Confucius (Kongzi, 551-479 BCE) taught a system of social ethics based on five key relationships: ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife, elder-younger sibling, friend-friend. Filial piety (xiao) anchors the family; ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety) anchor the broader ethical life.

The Analects (Lunyu) is the foundational text, compiled by disciples. Mencius (4th century BCE) and Xunzi (3rd century BCE) developed the tradition. Neo-Confucianism (Zhu Xi, 12th century) systematised it for later imperial China.

Whether Confucianism is a religion depends on the definition of religion — it includes ritual, sage veneration and cosmological elements but no creator god or afterlife doctrine.
items.why: Western categories ('religion', 'philosophy', 'ethics') don't always fit non-Western traditions. Confucianism's case shows how the very question of what counts as religion is partly a cultural artefact — and changes the answer.

items.title: The Five Pillars have a canonical order — beginning with Shahada
items.claim: What is the standard Sunni order of the Five Pillars of Islam?

options.text: Charity, fasting, prayer, pilgrimage, declaration
Shahada (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (almsgiving, 2.5% of accumulated wealth), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca, once if able)
Hajj, Salah, Sawm, Shahada, Zakat
There is no fixed order

items.reveal:
The Hadith of Gabriel (recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) lists the Pillars in this order. The Shahada is the doorway — 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God'.

Shia Islam (Twelver tradition) frames obligations differently. They recognise the practices but as part of the Furu al-Din (Ten Ancillaries of the Religion), alongside jihad, enjoining good and forbidding wrong, tawalla (love of the household of the Prophet) and tabarra (disassociation from enemies).

Zakat is calculated annually on accumulated wealth above a threshold (nisab); Sawm requires no food, drink or marital relations from dawn (fajr) to sunset (maghrib) during Ramadan.
items.why: Religious practice has specific structure. Treating the Pillars as a vague list of good acts misses the theological logic — faith first, then prayer, then social action.

items.title: The Sunni-Shia split began over political succession in 632 CE
items.claim: What is the origin of the Sunni-Shia division?

options.text: Two separate communities formed centuries apart in different countries

After Muhammad's death on 8 June 632 CE without a clear successor, those who supported Abu Bakr (chosen as first caliph) became Sunni; those who held Ali (Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law) had been designated became Shia — entrenched after Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE
A 19th-century theological dispute
A modern political invention

items.reveal:
Abu Bakr was chosen at Saqifah immediately after Muhammad's death. Umar (634-644), Uthman (644-656), then Ali (656-661) followed as the 'Rightly-Guided Caliphs'. Umar and Uthman were assassinated.

The First Fitna (civil war, 656-661) and Husayn ibn Ali's death at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) crystallised Shia identity. Husayn's grandfather was Muhammad; his death is mourned annually at Ashura.

Globally, around 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni, 10-15% Shia. Shia majorities: Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain. Significant minorities: Lebanon, Yemen, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India.
items.why: Major religious traditions can be shaped by political beginnings. The Sunni-Shia distinction is real and consequential — and originally a question about who should lead, not what to believe.

items.title: Muslims believe the Quran was revealed via the angel Gabriel
items.claim: How do Muslims understand the Quran's origin?

options.text: Muhammad's wise sayings, gathered over centuries
The direct word of God, revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) over 23 years (610-632 CE), to be recited and transmitted unchanged in Arabic
A revised version of the Bible adapted for Arabia
A book Muhammad composed himself

items.reveal:
The word 'Quran' comes from the Arabic root q-r-' meaning 'to recite'. The first revelation (Sura 96, 'Iqra' — 'Recite!') is dated to around 610 CE at the Cave of Hira on Mount Jabal al-Nour.

The Quran was compiled in written form under the third caliph Uthman (around 650 CE), with non-conforming versions destroyed to ensure a single authoritative text. Muslims regard only the Arabic text as the Quran proper; translations are 'meanings of' the Quran.

The Hadith — sayings of Muhammad — is a separate category, compiled by his companions and successors. Major Sunni collections: Sahih al-Bukhari (d. 870) and Sahih Muslim (d. 875).
items.why: The Quran's status differs from how Christians understand the Bible. Islamic theology treats every Arabic word as direct divine speech — which is why translation is always 'the meaning of' rather than 'the Quran'.

items.title: Jihad has greater and lesser meanings in classical Islam
items.claim: What is the greater/lesser jihad distinction?

options.text: Both refer only to armed warfare

A widely cited hadith distinguishes lesser jihad (armed struggle in defence of the community) from greater jihad (inner struggle against one's own ego); the hadith's authenticity is debated but the inner-struggle understanding is found in independent Sufi and mainstream piety traditions
Jihad means only physical exercise
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and some modern scholars question the hadith's chain of authentication. But the inner-struggle theme appears widely in Sufi writing and is not dependent on the hadith alone.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations of the term.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: Ramadan moves through the year on the lunar calendar
items.claim: Why does Ramadan fall in different seasons across years?

options.text: It is fixed each year by Islamic council

The Islamic (Hijri) calendar is purely lunar with no intercalation; its 12 months total around 354 days; Ramadan therefore shifts about 11 days earlier each Gregorian year, cycling through all seasons over around 33 years
It follows the solar year
It is fixed to August every year

items.reveal:
Most other religious calendars (Jewish, Hindu, Buddhist) are lunisolar — they add intercalary months to keep festivals in fixed seasons. The Islamic calendar deliberately rejects intercalation, based on Quran 9:36-37.

The Hijri year begins from Muhammad's emigration (hijra) from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. The Hijri year 1446 began in July 2024.

In tropical countries Ramadan stays around 12-14 hours of fasting daylight; in high latitudes in summer it can exceed 20 hours, raising practical questions for which contemporary scholars give differing rulings.
items.why: Calendar choices have theological consequences. The Islamic refusal to align the lunar year with the seasons produces a religious experience that cycles through climates and seasons — different from Christianity or Judaism.

items.title: Hajj is required once in a lifetime if able
items.claim: What is Hajj and when is it performed?

options.text: An annual pilgrimage required of all Muslims every year

Pilgrimage to Mecca performed in the month of Dhul Hijjah, required once in a lifetime if physically and financially able; around 2 million pilgrims attend annually, performing rites including circling the Kaaba (tawaf), running between Safa and Marwa (sa'i), and standing at Arafat
A weekly pilgrimage to the local mosque
Hajj is performed only by women

items.reveal:
Hajj takes place from 8 to 12 Dhul Hijjah, the last month of the Islamic year. Pilgrims enter ihram (a state of consecration, marked by white seamless cloth for men) and perform specific rites: tawaf around the Kaaba (seven times), sa'i between the hills of Safa and Marwa (in commemoration of Hagar), and standing at Arafat (wuquf) on 9 Dhul Hijjah.

Umrah is a 'lesser pilgrimage' that can be done any time of year.

Saudi Arabia issues quotas to each country to manage capacity. Crushes during stoning of the Jamarat (most famously 2015, around 2,400 dead) have driven major infrastructure changes.
items.why: Hajj is the largest annual gathering of humans in one place. Its scale and ritual specificity bring together Muslims from every nation — a deliberate religious enactment of global community.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible
items.claim: What is the Torah?

options.text: Only the book of Genesis
The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash; the first section of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)
The entire Old Testament
A modern compilation of prayers

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) is structured in three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books in Jewish count), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). 'Tanakh' is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in an annual cycle (some Reform congregations use a triennial cycle). The cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The Written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' is often used loosely. Students need to distinguish Torah (5 books) from Tanakh (24 books) from Talmud (rabbinic commentary) — and notice that the Christian Old Testament has the same content but in different order.

items.title: Pesach commemorates the Exodus from Egypt
items.claim: What does Pesach (Passover) celebrate?

options.text: The giving of the Torah at Sinai
The Exodus from Egyptian slavery — the angel of death 'passing over' Jewish homes marked with lamb's blood, the hasty departure (unleavened bread, matzah), the crossing of the Red Sea
The destruction of the Second Temple
The autumn harvest

items.reveal:
Pesach falls on 15 Nisan (March-April). It lasts 7 days in Israel (and for Reform Jews worldwide), 8 days in the Diaspora for Orthodox and Conservative Jews.

The Seder is the ritual meal on the first night (and second night in the Diaspora). The Haggadah ('the telling') is recited — recounting the Exodus through symbolic foods (matzah, maror, charoset), four cups of wine, and the four questions (asked by the youngest).

The festival ends with 'Next year in Jerusalem'. Its liberation theme has shaped social movements: African American spirituals (Go Down Moses), the Civil Rights movement (King invoked Exodus), Latin American liberation theology.
items.why: Judaism's major festivals carry specific historical content. Pesach is not generic 'spring festival' but structured ritual recreation of a specific liberation narrative — central to Jewish identity for over two millennia.

items.title: Kosher laws separate meat and dairy in cooking, eating and utensils
items.claim: What are the main kashrut restrictions?

options.text: Only vegetarian foods are permitted

Permitted animals (mammals chewing cud with cloven hooves; fish with fins and scales); ritual slaughter (shechita) by a trained shochet; separation of meat and dairy; prohibitions including pork, shellfish and mixing milk and meat
Only meals at synagogue must be kosher
Kosher refers only to wine

items.reveal:
The meat-dairy separation derives from three repetitions of 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). Rabbinic interpretation extended this to all mixing.

Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 list permitted and forbidden animals. Pork and shellfish are the most widely known prohibitions; rabbit, camel and birds of prey are also forbidden.

Shechita is ritual slaughter by a perfectly sharp knife in a single cut, designed to be quick and to drain blood. Some European countries (Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Belgian regions, Denmark) have banned shechita without prior stunning on animal-welfare grounds — a continuing source of dispute.
items.why: Religious practice is often embodied — daily eating, household kitchens, separate dishes. Kashrut is one of the clearest cases of belief expressed through bodily and domestic practice.

items.title: The Abrahamic covenant is sealed by circumcision
items.claim: What is the Abrahamic covenant?

options.text: A modern theological invention
The covenant between God and Abraham (Genesis 17) promising land and descendants, sealed by circumcision (brit milah) on the eighth day — still observed for Jewish boys today
A treaty between Jewish tribes
Applies only to ancient Israel

items.reveal:
Brit milah is performed on the eighth day after birth by a mohel. It marks the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:11-13).

The Mosaic covenant at Sinai (around 1300 BCE in traditional dating) establishes the 613 mitzvot of the Torah law — the framework for Jewish practice.

The Noahide covenant (Genesis 9) applies to all humanity. Rabbinic Judaism distinguishes seven Noahide laws binding on all people from the 613 mitzvot specifically binding on Jews.

Christianity reinterprets these covenants through 'new covenant' theology (Hebrews 8); Judaism rejects supersessionism — the older covenants are not abrogated.
items.why: Covenant is not vague relationship language. In Judaism it is a specific structure with terms, obligations and consequences — and a major point of theological disagreement with Christianity.

items.title: Modern Judaism has Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist branches
items.claim: What distinguishes the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: There are no real denominational differences

Orthodox (Modern Orthodox, Haredi), Conservative (Masorti in UK), Reform, and Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and engagement with modernity
Catholic and Protestant Jews
Only ethnic, not religious, divisions

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Modern Orthodox (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging modern life. Haredi (often called 'ultra-Orthodox') resists much of modernity.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as an evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in structurally different ways.

items.title: Shabbat begins on Friday evening and ends on Saturday night
items.claim: When does the Jewish Sabbath begin and end?

options.text: Saturday morning to Sunday morning
From sunset on Friday to the appearance of three stars on Saturday night — Jewish days begin at sunset, following Genesis 1's 'and there was evening and there was morning'
Calculated by the Gregorian clock
Runs continuously all weekend

items.reveal:
The Genesis creation account marks each day 'there was evening and there was morning'. Jewish days begin at sunset. Shabbat is welcomed with candle lighting (typically 18 minutes before sunset) and Kiddush over wine.

The Torah commands rest from melacha — 39 categories of work derived from activities involved in building the Tabernacle. These include lighting fires, writing, carrying in public, tearing, cooking. Modern applications (electricity, driving, mobile phones) follow rabbinic reasoning by analogy.

Shabbat ends with Havdalah — a brief ceremony with wine, spices and a multi-wick candle marking the separation between holy and ordinary time.
items.why: Religious time is structured differently. Treating Shabbat as 'Saturday' misses both its beginning at sunset and the depth of its observance — one of the most distinctive elements of Jewish practice.

items.title: The Four Noble Truths are framed like a medical diagnosis
items.claim: What are the Four Noble Truths of Buddhism?

options.text: Compassion, generosity, mindfulness, patience
Dukkha (suffering exists), Samudaya (its cause is craving/tanha), Nirodha (it can cease), Magga (the path — the Eightfold Path)
Birth, illness, ageing, death
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort

items.reveal:
The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths in his first sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) at Sarnath, near Varanasi, after his enlightenment. They are structured as a medical diagnosis: symptom, cause, prognosis, treatment.

'Dukkha' is often translated 'suffering' but covers unsatisfactoriness — the inability of conditioned things to give lasting peace. 'Tanha' is craving, including for existence and non-existence.

The Eightfold Path is grouped into wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, action, livelihood) and mental discipline (right effort, mindfulness, concentration).
items.why: Buddhism is often summarised as 'life is suffering' — a misleading reduction. The Four Noble Truths are a structured argument from problem to solution, not a pessimistic mood.

items.title: The Eightfold Path has three groups: wisdom, conduct, discipline
items.claim: How is the Eightfold Path structured?

options.text: Eight separate sequential stages

Eight factors in three groups: wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, right action, right livelihood), mental discipline (right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration) — practised together, not sequentially
Eight different deities to worship
Eight commandments from the Buddha

items.reveal:
The Eightfold Path (ariya atthangika magga) is the content of the Fourth Noble Truth. The three groups (panna/sila/samadhi — wisdom, ethics, mental discipline) reinforce each other.

'Right' (samma) means complete or perfect rather than morally correct in a narrow sense. Right View includes understanding the Four Noble Truths; right intention includes renunciation and non-cruelty.

Right Livelihood excludes specific occupations: trading in weapons, living beings (slavery), meat (butcher), intoxicants, poisons. Right Mindfulness is the practice that secular mindfulness movements have isolated from its Buddhist context.
items.why: The Eightfold Path is not a sequential checklist. The three trainings work together — and modern adaptations (secular mindfulness) often extract one element from a framework designed to be integrated.

items.title: Buddhism does not teach a creator god
items.claim: Does classical Buddhism teach a supreme creator deity?

options.text: Yes, the Buddha is worshipped as supreme deity
No — classical Buddhism rejects an eternal creator god; gods (devas) may exist but are themselves caught in samsara; liberation depends on the Eightfold Path, not divine grace
Yes, Brahma is the Buddhist supreme being
Only Mahayana affirms a creator god

items.reveal:
In the Pali Canon, the Buddha refuses metaphysical speculation about a creator (e.g. the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta, the 'parable of the poisoned arrow'). Devas exist but are impermanent and themselves seek liberation. The path to nibbana does not depend on grace from a supreme being.

Later traditions (Pure Land, some Mahayana schools) develop devotional practice toward Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but these are still not creators in the Abrahamic sense.

The Buddha is not a god — he is an awakened human teacher. Buddha statues are reminders, not objects of worship as deity.
items.why: Western definitions of religion centre on theism. Buddhism is a major world tradition that fits awkwardly inside that frame — and forces a rethink of what 'religion' even means.

items.title: Buddhism teaches anatta — no permanent self
items.claim: What is the doctrine of anatta?

options.text: The soul is eternal and unchanging
There is no permanent, unchanging self (atman); what we call 'self' is a constantly changing aggregation of five skandhas (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness)
Only the body is real; the soul is illusion
Each person has multiple souls

items.reveal:
Anatta (no-self) is one of the three marks of existence in Buddhism, alongside anicca (impermanence) and dukkha (unsatisfactoriness). The doctrine sharply distinguishes Buddhism from Hinduism's atman/Brahman teaching.
