The Anattalakkhana Sutta — the Buddha's second sermon — argues each of the five skandhas is impermanent and not under our control, so cannot be 'self'.

Later Mahayana schools developed the concept further. Yogacara introduced 'alaya-vijnana' (storehouse consciousness); some Pure Land traditions speak of 'Buddha-nature' that complicates the picture without abandoning anatta.
items.why: Anatta is one of the most counter-intuitive religious doctrines. It contradicts both Western theological assumptions about the soul and lived experience of continuity — and is the central philosophical claim of Buddhism.

items.title: Theravada and Mahayana are the two major Buddhist traditions
items.claim: How do Theravada and Mahayana differ?

options.text: They are unrelated religions

Theravada ('teaching of the elders') dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos — emphasises the Pali Canon and arhat ideal; Mahayana ('great vehicle') dominant in East Asia and Vietnam — emphasises bodhisattva path and Sanskrit/Chinese sutras; Tibetan Vajrayana is sometimes treated as a third stream
Both are identical to Hinduism
Mahayana rejects the Buddha

items.reveal:
The split developed in the centuries after the Buddha's death, with the Second Council (around 100 years after his parinirvana) marking early disagreements. Mahayana texts (Prajnaparamita Sutras, Lotus Sutra) emerged from around the 1st century BCE.

The bodhisattva ideal — postponing one's own final liberation to help all beings — is central to Mahayana. Theravada acknowledges bodhisattvas (including the historical Buddha before his enlightenment) but emphasises the arhat ideal.

Tibetan Buddhism is often treated as a separate Vajrayana branch. Zen and Pure Land are East Asian Mahayana developments.
items.why: Calling Buddhism 'one religion' obscures real diversity. The traditions share core teachings but differ on the path, the goal, the authoritative texts, and the role of devotion.

items.title: Vedantic Hinduism teaches the unity of atman and Brahman
items.claim: What does 'tat tvam asi' mean?

options.text: Soul and god are entirely separate

'That thou art' (Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7) — atman (the individual self) is identical with, or in relation to, Brahman (ultimate reality); different Vedanta schools interpret the relationship as non-dual, qualified non-dual, or dualist
Only Brahman is real; atman is illusion with no relation
Brahman is a god subordinate to atman

items.reveal:
The Mahavakyas ('great sayings') include 'tat tvam asi' (Chandogya 6.8.7), 'aham brahmasmi' (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10), 'ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2).

Shankara (8th century CE) developed Advaita Vedanta — non-duality: atman is identical to Brahman; perceived multiplicity is maya (illusion).

Ramanuja (11th-12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita — qualified non-duality: atman is a real attribute of Brahman but distinct. Madhva (13th century) taught Dvaita — full dualism: souls and God are eternally distinct.

All three schools are orthodox Vedantic positions.
items.why: Hindu philosophy of self is sophisticated. Treating Hinduism as 'just polytheism' misses the metaphysical core that has shaped Indian thought for over two millennia.

items.title: Samsara, karma and moksha form a connected Hindu framework
items.claim: How do these concepts relate?

options.text: Unrelated concepts

Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; karma is the moral causation that drives it; moksha is liberation from the cycle — typically via realisation of the unity of atman and Brahman, or through bhakti devotion
Karma punishes only in this life
Moksha is automatic at death for all souls

items.reveal:
Karma (action) produces fruits (phala) that bind the soul to future rebirths. Bad karma leads to lower rebirths (animal, hell realms); good karma to better ones (human, deva). All rebirth is conditioned and impermanent.

Moksha is the exit from samsara — variously achieved through jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (right action), or yoga (meditation). The Bhagavad Gita presents all four as legitimate paths.

Buddhism shares samsara, karma and liberation concepts but rejects atman — so 'rebirth' in Buddhism is the continuation of a causal stream, not a soul transmigrating.
items.why: Indian-origin religions share a family of concepts that differ in detail but contrast structurally with Abrahamic religions. The cyclic worldview shapes everything from ethics to attitudes toward death.

items.title: Hindu deities are often understood as manifestations of one Brahman
items.claim: How does Hindu theology relate the many gods to Brahman?

options.text: Each god is wholly separate and independent

Many Hindus understand the gods as manifestations (devas) of one ultimate reality (Brahman) — though the relationship varies between traditions; the Rig Veda (1.164.46) says 'Truth is one; sages call it by many names'
There is only one god — Brahma alone
Hinduism is strictly atheist

items.reveal:
The Trimurti (Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer) is one classical mapping of cosmic functions.

Vaishnavism centres on Vishnu and his avatars (Rama, Krishna). Shaivism centres on Shiva. Shaktism centres on Devi/Shakti (the divine feminine — Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati). Each tradition may treat its chosen deity as supreme.

The term 'henotheism' (worshipping one god while acknowledging others) was coined by Max Müller in the 19th century specifically to describe Vedic religion.
items.why: Calling Hinduism polytheistic or monotheistic both miss the structure. The 'many manifestations of one' framework is philosophically distinct — and shapes how Hindus actually relate to images and shrines.

items.title: Dharma is a central but multi-layered Hindu concept
items.claim: What does 'dharma' mean in Hinduism?

options.text: Just 'religion' in the modern sense

A complex term combining duty, righteousness, cosmic order and the proper way of life — context-specific (sva-dharma, one's own duty), stage-of-life-specific (ashrama dharma), and universal (sanatana dharma)
A type of meditation
A Hindu deity

items.reveal:
The root dhr- means 'to hold' or 'sustain'. Dharma includes the cosmic order (rita in Vedic terms), social duty (varna dharma — duties of one's caste), age-appropriate duty (ashrama dharma — student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer), and universal moral law (sanatana dharma).

The Bhagavad Gita (around 2nd century BCE) is the most influential text on dharma. Arjuna's crisis on the battlefield turns on the conflict between his duty as warrior (his sva-dharma) and his reluctance to kill kinsmen.

Krishna teaches that performing one's dharma without attachment to results (karma yoga) is the path to liberation.
items.why: Dharma has no single English equivalent. Translating it as 'religion' or 'duty' alone misses the richness — it shapes how Hindus understand both individual choice and cosmic order.

items.title: Varna (theory) and jati (lived caste) are not identical
items.claim: What is the relationship between varna and jati?

options.text: They are the same thing

Varna is the fourfold theoretical division (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) described in the Vedas and Manusmriti; jati is the thousands of birth-based occupational groupings that form the lived caste system; Dalits ('untouchables') were outside the four varnas
Caste is purely social with no religious dimension
Caste was invented by British colonisers

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta (10.90) describes the four varnas emerging from a cosmic being. The Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE-200 CE) codifies caste duties.

B. R. Ambedkar (1891-1956), Dalit leader and chief architect of India's constitution, converted to Buddhism in 1956 with around 500,000 followers, partly to escape caste. The Indian Constitution (1950) outlaws untouchability.

The relationship between varna theory and the thousands of jatis on the ground is complex and historically contested. Caste discrimination persists in many forms; the UK Equality Act 2010 includes caste under race discrimination provisions.
items.why: Religious texts and social systems interact in ways that resist clean separation. The caste case shows how a tradition can be deployed for social hierarchy and also generate its own critics.

items.title: Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak in 1469
items.claim: Who founded Sikhism and what did he teach?

options.text: Guru Arjan in 1604

Guru Nanak (born 1469 at Nankana Sahib, in modern Pakistan) taught one God (Ek Onkar), equality of all people regardless of caste or gender, honest work (kirat karna), sharing with others (vand chakna), and remembrance of God (naam japna)
A 19th-century reform movement
A breakaway sect of Islam

items.reveal_title: There is neither Hindu nor Muslim
items.reveal:
Born in 1469 at Nankana Sahib, Nanak had a transformative spiritual experience in 1499 — after emerging from three days at the Bein river he reportedly said 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim', pointing past religious labels to a shared underlying truth.

He undertook four major journeys (udasis) across India, into Tibet, the Middle East and possibly to Mecca. He died in 1539.

The Mool Mantar — Sikhism's foundational statement — begins 'Ik Onkar': there is one God. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with it.
items.why: Sikhism is the youngest of the major Indian religions — a deliberate rethinking of religious identity in Mughal-era Punjab. Its founding moment is well-attested historically, unlike older religions.

items.title: Ten human Sikh Gurus, then the eternal Guru Granth Sahib
items.claim: How does the Sikh tradition handle leadership after Guru Gobind Singh?

options.text: It ended with the tenth Guru with no continuation
In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh declared the Guru Granth Sahib (the scripture) to be the eternal Guru — no further human gurus
It continues through a hereditary line
Multiple gurus operate simultaneously today

items.reveal:
Guru Gobind Singh died in 1708 from a stab wound inflicted by an Afghan assassin. Before his death he installed the Adi Granth (compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604) as Guru Granth Sahib — making the scripture the eternal Guru.

The Guru Granth Sahib (1,430 pages, mostly in Gurmukhi script) contains hymns by six of the ten Gurus, plus 15 Hindu and Muslim saints (bhagats) — including Kabir and Sheikh Farid. It is treated as a living Guru: bowed to, awakened in the morning, put to rest at night.

Sikh gurdwaras place the Guru Granth Sahib on a throne (palki) as the central focus.
items.why: The structural innovation of designating scripture as eternal Guru ended succession disputes that plague many religions. Sikh community continuity rests on the text, not on a living hierarchy.

items.title: The Khalsa was founded at Vaisakhi 1699
items.claim: What did Guru Gobind Singh establish in 1699?

options.text: A new Sikh state in northern India

The Khalsa ('the pure') — a community of initiated Sikhs marked by the Five Ks (Kesh, Kara, Kanga, Kachera, Kirpan), open to all castes and genders, with surnames Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women
A revised version of the Guru Granth Sahib
A peace treaty with the Mughal Empire

items.reveal:
At Anandpur on Vaisakhi (April) 1699, Guru Gobind Singh called for volunteers willing to die for the faith. The Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) came forward, were initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword), and were then themselves used to initiate Gobind Singh.

The Five Ks: Kesh (uncut hair, including the dastaar turban), Kara (steel bracelet), Kanga (wooden comb), Kachera (cotton undergarment), Kirpan (small sword).

The Khalsa took the surnames Singh and Kaur, symbolically equalising caste and gender.
items.why: Sikh identity has visible bodily markers from a specific 1699 event with named participants. The Five Ks are not vague cultural symbols but coded responses to Mughal-era persecution and caste hierarchy.

items.title: Every Sikh gurdwara serves langar — a free meal for all
items.claim: What is langar?

options.text: A meal sold to support the gurdwara

A free communal meal served to anyone regardless of religion, caste, gender or background — a foundational Sikh practice originated by Guru Nanak and institutionalised by Guru Amar Das (3rd Guru), who required visitors to eat langar before meeting him
A festival meal only
Restricted to initiated Khalsa Sikhs

items.reveal:
Langar is served in the langar hall of every gurdwara worldwide. All sit on the floor at the same level — explicitly rejecting caste hierarchy. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar) serves around 100,000 meals daily; volunteers prepare and clean.

Guru Amar Das (1479-1574) made eating langar a requirement before meeting him — including for the Mughal Emperor Akbar, who reportedly sat with peasants before being granted an audience.

In the UK, Sikh organisations like Khalsa Aid extend the langar tradition to refugees, food banks and disaster response — in Ukraine, Turkey after the 2023 earthquake, and at UK floods.
items.why: Practice can teach doctrine. Sitting on the floor and eating together puts equality into the body — more direct than verbal teaching.

items.title: Aquinas offered Five Ways, not one argument
items.claim: What are Aquinas's Five Ways?

options.text: Five biblical proofs
Five distinct a posteriori arguments in Summa Theologiae I.2.3: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer)
A single ontological argument
Five mystical experiences

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes a priori arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from a posteriori arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move; an unmoved mover is required. Second Way (efficient causation): a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised separately. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's exchange with Copleston (1948 BBC debate) challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.

items.title: Anselm's ontological argument is a priori
items.claim: What is Anselm's ontological argument (Proslogion, 1078)?

options.text: An empirical argument from nature
God is 'that than which no greater can be conceived'; existence in reality is greater than existence in the mind alone; therefore the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality
A historical argument from miracles
An argument from religious experience

items.reveal:
Anselm wrote the Proslogion (1077-78) as a contemplation aimed at finding 'a single argument' to prove God's existence. The famous formula appears in Proslogion 2.

Gaunilo, Anselm's contemporary, objected with his 'lost island' parody: by the same logic, the greatest conceivable island must exist. Anselm replied that the argument applies only to a necessary being, not to contingent ones.

Descartes (Meditations V), Spinoza, Leibniz and Hegel reformulated versions. Kant's critique — existence is not a predicate (Critique of Pure Reason, 1781) — is the standard counter. Alvin Plantinga's modal version (1974) revived the argument using possible-world semantics.
items.why: The ontological argument is uniquely controversial. Almost everyone has the intuition that something is wrong with it — but the precise diagnosis (Gaunilo's? Kant's? Modal logic?) is itself contested philosophy.

items.title: Paley's watchmaker argument (1802) was anticipated by Hume's critique
items.claim: What is Paley's design argument and how did Hume respond?

options.text: Paley accepted Hume's criticism and abandoned the design argument

Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) argued from the complexity of a found watch to a designer, by analogy with biology. Hume's 'Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion' (1779, posthumous) had already attacked the analogy — universe is unlike a watch, the analogy points to an apprentice or committee of designers, not a single benevolent God
Hume defended a stronger version of the argument
Paley wrote in 1700, before Hume

items.reveal:
William Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) opens with the watch-on-the-heath analogy. He uses the human eye as his prime biological example.

Hume's 'Dialogues' (1779, published posthumously) anticipated and refuted versions of the design argument decades earlier. Three main lines: the universe is not closely analogous to a watch; the analogy could equally suggest a committee, apprentice or evil designer; the argument cannot reach a single benevolent God of classical theism.

Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) provided a non-design explanation for biological complexity. Modern Intelligent Design (Behe, Dembski, 1990s onwards) is a controversial attempt to revive the argument scientifically.
items.why: The design argument keeps returning in new forms. Each version has to deal with the next development in science — biological evolution, cosmic fine-tuning, multiverse cosmology — making it a moving target rather than a settled debate.

items.title: Moral and natural evil are distinct problems for theism
items.claim: What is the distinction between moral and natural evil?

options.text: All evil is caused by human moral failure

Moral evil is caused by free moral agents (murder, torture, cruelty); natural evil is caused by impersonal natural processes (earthquakes, disease, predation) — they raise different problems for theistic theodicies
All evil is illusion
Natural evil is just a subset of moral evil

items.reveal:
Free Will Defence (Augustine, Alvin Plantinga) explains moral evil as the cost of human free will — but doesn't obviously address natural evil. Earthquakes do not flow from human choices.

Irenaean theodicy (revived by John Hick, 'Evil and the God of Love', 1966) sees natural evil as part of soul-making — character development requires a challenging environment.

Augustinian theodicy treats evil as privatio boni (privation of good) — not a substance but an absence. The Fall extends moral consequences into nature.

The logical problem of evil (J. L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', 1955) has been largely answered by Plantinga's free-will defence; the evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979) remains live.
items.why: The problem of evil is the most persistent challenge to classical theism. The moral/natural and logical/evidential distinctions shape which theodicies are even relevant — generic answers miss the structure of the argument.

items.title: Wittgenstein treated religious language as a 'language game'
items.claim: How did the later Wittgenstein approach religious language?

options.text: He argued religious language is meaningless
Religious language is a 'language game' embedded in a 'form of life' — it has its own grammar, not reducible to scientific assertion; meaningful within its practice
He defended a literal cognitive interpretation
He treated all language games as equally true

items.reveal:
Wittgenstein's 'Philosophical Investigations' (published 1953) replaced the picture theory of meaning from his earlier 'Tractatus' (1921) with a use-theory: 'the meaning of a word is its use in the language'.

Religious language games — prayer, worship, doctrinal assertion — function differently from scientific language games. D. Z. Phillips and Norman Malcolm developed Wittgensteinian philosophy of religion in the 20th century.

Critics (Antony Flew, 'Theology and Falsification' 1950) argued this reduces religious claims to non-cognitive expressions; defenders argue Wittgenstein himself was more nuanced, refusing both literalist and reductionist readings.
items.why: 20th-century philosophy of religion shifted from 'do these claims correspond to reality?' to 'what kind of claims are these?'. Wittgenstein opens space for religious practice without requiring scientific-style verification.

items.title: Act and rule utilitarianism produce different answers
items.claim: What is the act-rule distinction in utilitarianism?

options.text: Identical theories under different names

Act utilitarianism judges each action by its direct consequences; rule utilitarianism asks which rules, if generally followed, would maximise utility — and applies those rules even when an individual act might seem to give a different answer
Rule utilitarianism rejects consequences entirely
Act utilitarianism is the only legitimate form

items.reveal:
Jeremy Bentham's 'Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789) introduced the hedonic calculus. John Stuart Mill's 'Utilitarianism' (1861) distinguished higher and lower pleasures.

Rule utilitarianism (developed by R. M. Hare and Richard Brandt in the 20th century) attempts to address objections to act utilitarianism — that it permits horrific acts (killing one innocent to save five) and creates impossible decision burdens.

Critics argue rule utilitarianism collapses into act utilitarianism (just add 'except in special cases') or into Kantian deontology (just follow the rules).
items.why: Utilitarianism is not one theory. The act/rule distinction changes the answers radically — and exam answers that treat 'utilitarianism' as monolithic miss the most important internal debate.

items.title: Kant gave multiple formulations of the categorical imperative
items.claim: How does Kant's categorical imperative work?

options.text: A single rule: do unto others as you would have them do to you

Multiple formulations including universalisability ('act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law') and humanity-as-end ('act so as to treat humanity, in your own person or another's, always as an end, never as a means only')
Whatever maximises happiness
An empirical rule derived from observation

items.reveal:
Kant's 'Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals' (1785) sets out the categorical imperative. Standard count: three formulations.

Formula of Universal Law: 'Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.'
Formula of Humanity: 'Act so as to treat humanity... always as an end, never as a means only.'
Formula of the Kingdom of Ends: 'Act according to the maxims of a member of a merely possible kingdom of ends.'

Kant's most famous example — lying to the murderer at the door — shows the strict reading: lying is universally impermissible.
items.why: Kantian ethics is sometimes reduced to 'don't lie'. The multiple formulations and the humanity-as-end principle are richer — and more humane — than the slogan suggests.

items.title: Aristotelian virtue ethics aims at eudaimonia (flourishing)
items.claim: What is eudaimonia in Aristotle's ethics?

options.text: A momentary feeling of happiness

Flourishing or living well — the proper end of human life. The virtues (excellences of character) are stable dispositions developed through habituation that enable a person to function well as a human being
Wealth and reputation
Religious salvation

items.reveal:
Aristotle's 'Nicomachean Ethics' (Book I) argues that all human action aims at some good; there must be a highest good — eudaimonia.

The ergon (function) argument: humans, like everything, have a characteristic function — rational activity in accordance with virtue. The virtues are not lists of good behaviours but stable dispositions developed through habituation.

The doctrine of the mean: each virtue lies between two vices (courage between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between miserliness and profligacy).

Alasdair MacIntyre's 'After Virtue' (1981) revived virtue ethics by arguing modern moral discourse has lost the framework that gives moral vocabulary its meaning.
items.why: Virtue ethics is not 'be a good person'. It is a structured theory with specific terms — function, habituation, the mean, flourishing — linking character to the good life in a way that act-based theories do not.

items.title: Natural Law has primary precepts and secondary rules
items.claim: What are Aquinas's primary precepts of natural law?

options.text: The Ten Commandments from Exodus

Five primary precepts identified by Aquinas: preservation of life, reproduction, education of offspring, living in society, worship of God — secondary precepts (specific moral rules) are derived by reason
Only one rule — do good and avoid evil
Only protection of life

items.reveal:
Aquinas's natural law theory appears in the Summa Theologiae I-II (Questions 90-97). The eternal law is God's plan; natural law is rational creatures' participation in it; human law derives specific rules.

The doctrine of double effect — an action with a foreseen bad consequence can be permissible if the bad effect is not intended, the act itself is not intrinsically wrong, and the good outweighs the bad — is a key application (used in modern bioethics, especially end-of-life care).

Natural law is the basis of Catholic moral teaching on contraception, abortion and end-of-life care. John Finnis and Germain Grisez developed 'New Natural Law' (from 1980).
items.why: Catholic ethics is not arbitrary doctrine — it rests on a developed rational framework. Engaging with natural law requires understanding the structure (primary, secondary, double effect) rather than treating it as a list of forbidden actions.

items.title: Joseph Fletcher's situation ethics centres on agape
items.claim: What is the central principle of Fletcher's situation ethics?

options.text: There are no moral rules whatsoever
The single absolute is agape (selfless love); all other rules are guidelines that can be overridden when love requires. Set out in 'Situation Ethics: The New Morality' (1966)
Maximise pleasure for the greatest number
Always follow biblical commands literally

items.reveal:
Fletcher's six propositions: (1) Only love is intrinsically good. (2) The ruling norm of Christian decision is love, not law. (3) Love and justice are the same — justice is love distributed. (4) Love wills the neighbour's good. (5) Only the end justifies the means. (6) Love's decisions are made situationally, not prescriptively.

Fletcher's four working principles: pragmatism, relativism, positivism, personalism.

The Vatican condemned situation ethics under Pius XII (1956, before Fletcher's book) and again in the 1990s. Critics argue 'love' as sole criterion is too vague; defenders argue agape has specific New Testament content that excludes self-interested 'love'.
items.why: Christian ethics in the mid-20th century split between absolutist and contextual approaches. Fletcher's situation ethics is a high-profile example of context-driven ethics — challenging the natural law tradition from within Christianity.
